purpose: Provide the basis of preparation and “how to read this report” guidance for IFRS S1/S2 sustainability-related financial disclosures. Establish scope, reporting boundary, connectivity to financial statements, key qualitative characteristics, and the approach to comparatives, estimates, judgements, and cross-referencing.
tone: Formal, standards-aligned, precise, and neutral. Use assurance-like phrasing that emphasizes completeness, neutrality, accuracy, and freedom from material error. Use cautious, risk-aware language for sensitive matters and forward-looking judgements. Avoid promotional or celebratory language; keep emphasis on methodology and governance of reporting.
level_of_detail: High-level principles plus practical mechanics. Provide enough detail to explain how disclosures were prepared, scoped, and connected to financial reporting, without duplicating detailed topic disclosures. Use short subsections to cover each general requirement topic explicitly.
paragraph_style: Start with a short scope and basis-of-preparation statement. Follow with a bulleted list of qualitative characteristics and preparation principles. Then explain standards alignment and how disclosures map to the core pillars (governance, strategy, risk management, metrics and targets). Use short, numbered subsections for specific general requirements (e.g., connected information, comparatives, timing/location, reporting entity/value chain, sources of guidance). Include clear cross-references to where details are located elsewhere in the report set.
sentence_style: Declarative, unambiguous sentences. Prefer active voice where responsibility is clear; use passive voice sparingly for standard-setting or externally defined requirements. Define terms before use. Keep sentences short-to-medium length; use parallel structure in lists. Use conditional language for estimates and forward-looking information (e.g., “may,” “could,” “is expected to,” “is subject to”).
preferred_evidence_style: Ground statements in references to applicable standards and internal reporting constructs (e.g., alignment with financial reporting boundary, policies, methods, and estimates). Use traceability via internal cross-references to other sections/appendices rather than embedding extensive evidence artifacts. Clearly flag when contextual information extends beyond the reporting period and why it is included.
table_usage: Use tables sparingly. Prefer bullets for principles and mechanics. Use compact tables only when they improve scanability (e.g., mapping of general requirements topics to where disclosures appear; summary of applicable standard components; grouped stakeholder categories; stepwise methodology overview). Keep tables simple, with short labels and line breaks for narrow layouts.
figure_usage: Optional. Use simple diagrams or tile/grid layouts only to summarize scoping elements, stakeholder groupings, or priority themes at a high level. Avoid complex visuals in this section; prioritize clarity and navigability.
pdf_layout_usage: Use a chapter opener block with a prominent section marker and title. Repeat the section title as a running header on subsequent pages. Maintain consistent margins and line spacing. Use whitespace to separate narrative from list blocks. Format cross-references inline (e.g., “Refer to …”) and keep them consistent. Ensure subsection headings are visually distinct and support scanning.
how_to_discuss_missing_data: State transparently when information is not available, incomplete, or still under development. Explain the reason (e.g., data limitations, boundary constraints, methodology maturity), the interim approach used (e.g., estimates, proxies, partial coverage), and the plan to improve (e.g., controls, systems, scope expansion). Clarify whether omissions could be material and how materiality was assessed. Avoid implying certainty where estimates are used.
what_to_avoid: Any organization-specific names, brands, report titles, or proprietary program names
Any specific dates, reporting years, edition labels, or publication timing statements
Any amounts, percentages, performance claims, achievements, awards, or comparative boasting
Any jurisdiction-specific legal commentary, incorporation history, or regulatory endorsement narratives
Any specific currencies, geographic footprint details, entity counts, or segment/product descriptions
Any committee names, role titles, or stakeholder labels that are unique to a particular organization
Any fixed list of external frameworks or tools presented as universally applicable; keep configurable
Any specific note/appendix numbering or identifiers; use generic cross-reference placeholders
Exact copied wording from any reference report
